canonical_rules.predicate_text: Malignant tumours exhibit marked morphological, molecular, and proteomic heterogeneity
canonical_rules.representative_verbatim: Malignant tumours show a marked degree of morphological, molecular and proteomic heterogeneity. This variability is closely related to microenvironmental factors and the location of the tumour. The activation of genetic alterations is very tissue-dependent and only few tumours have distinct genetic alterations. Importantly, the activation state of proteins and signaling factors is heterogeneous in the primary tumour and in metastases and recurrences. The molecular diagnosis based only on genetic alterations can lead to treatments with unpredictable responses, depending on the tumour location, such as the tumour response in melanomas versus colon carcinomas with BRAF mutations. Therefore, we understand that the correct evaluation of tumours requires a system that integrates both morphological, molecular and protein information in a clinical and pathological context, where intratumoral heterogeneity can be assessed. Thus, we propose the term 'tissunomics', where the diagnosis will be contextualised in each tumour based on the complementation of the pathological, molecular, protein expression, environmental cells and clinical data.

canonical_rules.predicate_text: SMT: genetic mutations accumulate in cells inducing clonal expansion -> malignant transformation characterised by growth independence and resistance to apoptosis
canonical_rules.representative_verbatim: The paradigm of cancer as a genetic disease has existed since the early 1970s. For the last 50 years, cancer has been explained according to the somatic mutation theory (SMT), which states that genetic mutations accumulate in cells by inducing clonal expansion. Following Darwinian-type evolution, an initial clone accumulates multiple mutations, resulting in malignant transformation characterised by growth independence and resistance to apoptosis. These clones have trunk and branch mutations, and may also have driver and passenger mutations. -18 During tumour progression and after chemotherapy or radiotherapy, genetic alterations accumulate to select for the bestadapted clone. Molecular heterogeneity has been described in renal adenocarcinoma, breast cancer and glioblastoma, among others. It is thought that these clones with greater proliferative advantages and resistance to local stresses then predominate. -24

Grouping together the evidence for these theories, it has been demonstrated that (i) many spontaneous somatic mutations accumulate in cells during their lifetime, (ii) oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes play a critical role in cancer development and (iii) environmental factors trigger cancer onset and progression. Regarding field cancerisation, some authors have proposed that cancer is a tissue disorder with similarities to abnormal embryonic development, while others propose that cancer is a consortium of clones and local factors. It is understood that a single clone cannot harbour all the genetic alterations required for the invasive and metastatic tumour phenotype and that several clones acquire malignant properties that, synergistically, allow cells to grow, invade and metastasise. This consortium of tumour cell clones and microenvironment cells includes leucocytes, lymphocytes, fibroblasts and endothelial cells. A minimum number of cells is also required for a clone to be biologically viable -a phenomenon known as the Allee effect. This clonal cooperation has been proposed in pancreatic and breast cancer and melanoma and for circulating tumour cell (CTC) clusters. -33

canonical_rules.predicate_text: BRAF inhibitors -> effective in melanoma with BRAF mutations
canonical_rules.representative_verbatim: Currently, precision oncology is based on the existence of alterations in certain specific therapeutic targets regardless of tumour location or type. Tumours with somatic mutations such as BRAF, EGFR or gene rearrangements such as ALK are considered therapeutic options regardless of tumour type or location, and tumours may even be characterised as BRAFomas or ALKomas. However, some clinical data have shown that, while BRAF inhibitors are effective in melanoma, the same inhibitors of the same BRAF mutations in colorectal cancer induce feedback loops in signalling pathways that can have a detrimental effect. Cell signalling pathways are also highly regulated, often dependent on numerous positive and negative feedback loops, which are specific to the cell type and tumour environment. For this reason, BRAF inhibition in colorectal cancer indirectly results in EGFR receptor activation and subsequent PI3K -Akt pathway activation. Similarly, ALK alterations and their inhibitors do not have the same clinical response in lung tumours as in neuroblastomas. Further examples are inhibitors of EGFR, HER2 and HER3, depending on the tumour type and location. In a recent basket clinical trial, not all tumours were affected by the same HER mutations, and response to the HER2 inhibitor (neratinib) varied in different tissues: for example, colorectal or bladder cancer with HER2 mutations did not respond. In summary, specific drug treatment depends on the tissue context.

However, some clinical data have shown that, while BRAF inhibitors are effective in melanoma, the same inhibitors of the same BRAF mutations in colorectal cancer induce feedback loops in signalling pathways that can have a detrimental effect. Cell signalling pathways are also highly regulated, often dependent on numerous positive and negative feedback loops, which are specific to the cell type and tumour environment. For this reason, BRAF inhibition in colorectal cancer indirectly results in EGFR receptor activation and subsequent PI3K -Akt pathway activation. Similarly, ALK alterations and their inhibitors do not have the same clinical response in lung tumours as in neuroblastomas. Further examples are inhibitors of EGFR, HER2 and HER3, depending on the tumour type and location. In a recent basket clinical trial, not all tumours were affected by the same HER mutations, and response to the HER2 inhibitor (neratinib) varied in different tissues: for example, colorectal or bladder cancer with HER2 mutations did not respond. In summary, specific drug treatment depends on the tissue context.

canonical_rules.predicate_text: mRNA-based expression studies have low reproducibility dependent on mRNA stability
canonical_rules.representative_verbatim: Molecular classification based on mRNA expression profiling of gene groups is a frequent approach to identify and classify molecular subtypes of tumours. One of the major achievements of molecular classification has been the subcategorisation according to prognosis, and it is instrumental for the identification of new genetic alterations. However, mRNA-based expression studies are often limited by a low reproducibility, depending on mRNA stability. Furthermore, single-cell sequencing approaches are not feasible in routine diagnostics. Currently, samples are sequenced as the bulk of tumour cells and therefore do not provide information on ITH. In addition to these technical issues, monitoring gene expression at the mRNA level does not necessarily correlate with the function of a protein within a cell, as many post-transcriptional modifications determine whether or not mRNA finally gives rise to a functional protein. Importantly, however, the different molecular subtypes based on enormous mRNA expression matrices can be validated according to protein or gene expression using just a few in-situ hybridisation or IHC probes in most molecular cancer subtypes (see Table 2).

canonical_rules.predicate_text: Breast carcinoma -> 6 molecular subtypes by mRNA expression profile: luminal A, luminal B, HER2+, basal-like, claudin-low, normal breast-like
canonical_rules.representative_verbatim: Breast carcinoma. According to the mRNA expression profile, six molecular subtypes are described: luminal A, luminal B, HER2 +, basal-like, claudin-low and normal breast-like. However, RNA signatures can vary dramatically between patients with the same molecular subtype 69 and, with the exception of the basal subtype, are not highly reproducible for diagnosis on microarray analysis. A high degree of ITH has been described, as assessed by immunohistochemical (IHC) studies, array-CGH studies 71 and massive parallel sequencing technologies. Given these problems in the exact diagnosis of breast cancer subtype by molecular characterisation, IHC-based characterisations are recommended as a diagnostic approach in most of the consensus oncology guidelines. Additional IHC staining helps to distinguish luminal A and B subtypes, such as GATA3 and FOXM. CK5 and EGFR expression define the basal subtype of breast cancer, and CD44 and Snail expression determine the claudin-low subtype. Finally, the normal breast-like subtype is defined by low expression of the above-mentioned markers and expression of factors such as CD36 in a low-grade histological tumour.

canonical_rules.predicate_text: Bladder cancer RNA genome-wide studies characterise two main molecular groups (basal and luminal subtypes) with prognostic and predictive impact
canonical_rules.representative_verbatim: Urothelial bladder carcinoma. Different molecular classifications are currently being explored. One of them, based on RNA genomewide studies, has characterised two main molecular groups of bladder cancer with prognostic and predictive impact. Group 1 basal subtype includes a subgroup of claudin-low and is characterised by expression of the basal cytokeratins CK5, CK14 and CD44. Group 2 luminal subtype has mutations of the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene and urothelial differentiation markers such as CK20, GATA3 and uroplakins. The luminal subtype has a more favourable prognosis than the basal subtype. Recently, a prospective multicentre validation study with a 12-gene signature progression score in nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer was demonstrated to have independent prognostic power beyond clinical and histopathological risk factors, and could help in stratifying patients to optimise treatment and followup. Other molecular alterations have also been described, such as FGFR3 mutations in 80%, PI3KCA mutations in approximately 20% and mutations in the core promoter region of the human telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) gene in up to 85% of bladder tumours. Interestingly, FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations have been demonstrated as biomarkers on liquid biopsy for disease surveillance for bladder cancer. Different cell cycle genes may be altered in invasive urothelial carcinoma, mainly tumour suppressor genes, including TP53, p16 and Rb. Finally, combinations of TP53, p21, p27 and pRb proved to be more precise in classifying bladder cancer patients into risk groups.

canonical_rules.representative_verbatim: Molecular tumour subtypes based on mRNA expression profiles often show discordance with protein expression levels, depending on the RNA stability and the area sampled. It is well known that RNA studies are problematic regarding reproducibility, and that protein expression shows the real functional status of the targets. A classic example is breast cancer, in which mRNA profiles can define at least six different molecular categories. While this can be used as a general classification scheme, only IHC or FISH analysis of proteins in tumour cells within the individual subgroup can provide the exact diagnosis to guide treatment and prognosis. Some reports 67 describe discord, when comparing mRNA and protein expression levels, of up to 50% of cases in HER2 status, and in more than 15% of cases when distinguishing between luminal A and luminal B.

canonical_rules.predicate_text: Multiple oncogenic events converge on cellular networks containing clinically targetable hubs (e.g., eIF4F complex)
canonical_rules.representative_verbatim: Systems biology encompasses tools that hold great promise for deciphering the vulnerabilities of the tumour ecosystem as a whole. Studies are based on the premise that multiple oncogenic events converge on a number of cellular networks that may contain essential or synthetically lethal clinically targetable hubs or factors, such as the eIF4F complex. Nonetheless, many contemporary systems biology approaches do not consider intratumour heterogeneity. This is relevant because key functional nodes within the metabolic, signal transduction and gene expression networks responsible for supporting the tumour phenotype are critically dependent on the heterogeneity of the tumour. These data can also help to classify tumours according to histopathological, biochemical and genomic features and thus help to tailor the diagnosis and clinical management to a patient's biological tumour profile. Accordingly, multidimensional molecular and gene expression data, which are associated with the response to antitumour treatments and clinical progress, are thought to facilitate the selection of patients who are more likely to respond to targeted or 'precise' therapies. -131 The availability of systemwide data in a variety of cancers is facilitating the development of approaches that go beyond the classic, reductionist paradigms that associate single genes with cellular phenotypes and functions. Systems biology approaches consider the interplay between multiple molecular factors that underpin phenotype development. Accordingly, rather than a genetic disease, cancer is now perceived as a disease of 'networks', and to fully grasp the complexity of the tumour ecosystem the networks driving cancer need to be mapped and their dynamics and evolution over time deciphered. Emerging data show that these cancer networks are constantly rewired in part by clonal interactions, changing microenvironments and the acquisition of novel molecular alterations that are largely induced by anticancer treatments. Therefore, minor subpopulations that are not readily detectable in bulk tumours or that can adapt to hostile environments may emerge following treatments that specifically target cancerdriving mutations present in the predominant tumour subpopulations. Thus, in the coming years, systems biology implementation may be crucial for (i) detailed, clinically oriented subclassification of cancer types, (ii) mapping of oncogenic networks and identification of the critical nodes to overcome the effects of ITH and (iii) informing future preclinical research and design of Phase I clinical trials by anticipating therapy response in silico and predicting the best targets for each patient and tumour (personalised cancer therapy or precision medicine).

findings.claim: Malignant tumours exhibit marked morphological, molecular, and proteomic heterogeneity
findings.verbatim_support: Malignant tumours show a marked degree of morphological, molecular and proteomic heterogeneity. This variability is closely related to microenvironmental factors and the location of the tumour. The activation of genetic alterations is very tissue-dependent and only few tumours have distinct genetic alterations. Importantly, the activation state of proteins and signaling factors is heterogeneous in the primary tumour and in metastases and recurrences. The molecular diagnosis based only on genetic alterations can lead to treatments with unpredictable responses, depending on the tumour location, such as the tumour response in melanomas versus colon carcinomas with BRAF mutations. Therefore, we understand that the correct evaluation of tumours requires a system that integrates both morphological, molecular and protein information in a clinical and pathological context, where intratumoral heterogeneity can be assessed. Thus, we propose the term 'tissunomics', where the diagnosis will be contextualised in each tumour based on the complementation of the pathological, molecular, protein expression, environmental cells and clinical data.

The molecular diagnosis based only on genetic alterations can lead to treatments with unpredictable responses, depending on the tumour location, such as the tumour response in melanomas versus colon carcinomas with BRAF mutations. Therefore, we understand that the correct evaluation of tumours requires a system that integrates both morphological, molecular and protein information in a clinical and pathological context, where intratumoral heterogeneity can be assessed. Thus, we propose the term 'tissunomics', where the diagnosis will be contextualised in each tumour based on the complementation of the pathological, molecular, protein expression, environmental cells and clinical data.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk (PMC6851567) establishes the conceptual basis for a multimodal tumour evaluation framework. Malignant tumours display marked morphological, molecular, and proteomic heterogeneity [S1], driven by microenvironmental factors and tumour location [S2]. Genetic alterations are tissue-dependent in their activation, with few tumours possessing truly distinct alterations [S3], and protein/signaling factor activation states are heterogeneous across primary tumours, metastases, and recurrences [S4]. Relying solely on genetic alterations for molecular diagnosis can yield unpredictable treatment responses depending on tumour location [S5] — exemplified by divergent BRAF mutation responses in melanoma versus colon carcinoma [S5]. Accordingly, correct tumour evaluation is proposed to require integrated morphological, molecular, protein, and clinical assessment that accounts for intratumoral heterogeneity [S6]. The authors propose the term 'tissunomics' to describe this context-specific, multi-domain diagnostic approach [S7].

findings.claim: SMT: genetic mutations accumulate in cells inducing clonal expansion -> malignant transformation characterised by growth independence and resistance to apoptosis
findings.verbatim_support: The paradigm of cancer as a genetic disease has existed since the early 1970s. For the last 50 years, cancer has been explained according to the somatic mutation theory (SMT), which states that genetic mutations accumulate in cells by inducing clonal expansion. Following Darwinian-type evolution, an initial clone accumulates multiple mutations, resulting in malignant transformation characterised by growth independence and resistance to apoptosis. These clones have trunk and branch mutations, and may also have driver and passenger mutations. -18 During tumour progression and after chemotherapy or radiotherapy, genetic alterations accumulate to select for the bestadapted clone. Molecular heterogeneity has been described in renal adenocarcinoma, breast cancer and glioblastoma, among others. It is thought that these clones with greater proliferative advantages and resistance to local stresses then predominate. -24

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk introduces the somatic mutation theory (SMT) as the dominant paradigm for cancer biology since the early 1970s [S1–S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819]. Under SMT, accumulating genetic mutations drive clonal expansion and ultimately malignant transformation, characterised by growth independence and apoptosis resistance [S2–S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819]. Tumour clones are further distinguished by trunk/branch and driver/passenger mutations [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819]. Genetic alterations continue to accumulate during tumour progression and in response to chemotherapy or radiotherapy, selecting for the best-adapted clone [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819]. Molecular heterogeneity—a key consequence of this Darwinian evolution—has been documented in renal adenocarcinoma, breast cancer, and glioblastoma [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819], with clones bearing proliferative and stress-resistance advantages ultimately predominating [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819].

findings.claim: TOFT postulates neoplasia arises from local tissue disorder due to defect in cell-tissue component interaction; epigenetic or genetic changes affect both epithelial and stromal cells in multiple locations
findings.verbatim_support: Other theories include the tissue organisation field theory (TOFT), which postulates that neoplasia arises from a local tissue disorder and may be due to a defect in interaction between cells and other tissue components, -27 where epigenetic or genetic changes affect both epithelial and stromal cells in multiple locations. Grouping together the evidence for these theories, it has been demonstrated that (i) many spontaneous somatic mutations accumulate in cells during their lifetime, (ii) oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes play a critical role in cancer development and (iii) environmental factors trigger cancer onset and progression. Regarding field cancerisation, some authors have proposed that cancer is a tissue disorder with similarities to abnormal embryonic development, while others propose that cancer is a consortium of clones and local factors. It is understood that a single clone cannot harbour all the genetic alterations required for the invasive and metastatic tumour phenotype and that several clones acquire malignant properties that, synergistically, allow cells to grow, invade and metastasise. This consortium of tumour cell clones and microenvironment cells includes leucocytes, lymphocytes, fibroblasts and endothelial cells. A minimum number of cells is also required for a clone to be biologically viable -a phenomenon known as the Allee effect. This clonal cooperation has been proposed in pancreatic and breast cancer and melanoma and for circulating tumour cell (CTC) clusters. -33

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk reviews theoretical frameworks underpinning cancer development with a focus on field cancerisation and clonal evolution. The Tissue Organisation Field Theory (TOFT) proposes that neoplasia arises from local tissue disorder through defective cell–tissue interactions, with epigenetic/genetic changes affecting both epithelial and stromal cells at multiple locations [S1]. Consolidating evidence across theories confirms that: (i) spontaneous somatic mutations accumulate lifelong, (ii) oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes are critical drivers of cancer, and (iii) environmental factors trigger cancer onset and progression [S2]. Field cancerisation is conceptualised either as a tissue disorder resembling abnormal embryonic development or as a consortium of clones influenced by local factors [S3]. Crucially, no single clone contains all genetic alterations needed for invasion and metastasis; multiple clones synergistically cooperate to achieve the malignant phenotype [S4]. The tumour consortium encompasses not only tumour cell clones but also microenvironmental cells including leucocytes, lymphocytes, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells [S5]. Clonal viability requires a minimum cell number, described as the Allee effect [S6]. Clonal cooperation has been documented in pancreatic cancer, breast cancer, melanoma, and CTC clusters [S7].

findings.claim: APC gene alterations observed specifically in colorectal cancer
findings.verbatim_support: Certain genetic alterations are only observed in the context of specific cell or tissue types; 34 for example, alterations in the APC gene in colorectal cancer, CDH1 (E-cadherin) in gastric carcinoma, the VHL gene in renal carcinoma or BCR/ABL in leukaemia. These specific genetic alterations demonstrate that tissue type plays a role, which is currently not well understood and is under intensive investigation. The higher incidence of certain somatic mutations in some cell types might be explained by a cell- or tissue-specific chromosome disposition during interphase. This, along with epigenetic imprinting, may serve as a mechanism of gene regulation and allow differential access of carcinogens to certain DNA regions, resulting in a higher probability of mutations and specific rearrangements in some cells but not others. Similarly, the accessibility of certain chromosomal regions might explain cell-type-specific chromosomal translocations such as BCR/ABL in leucocytes or VHL mutations in renal cell carcinoma. Some mutations and genetic alterations are uniformly present in the entire organism, such as germline mutations, BRCA1 and BRCA2, VHL in Von Hippel Lindau syndrome and as many as 30 others, but they are usually only associated with tumours in specific tissues, such as BRCA1/2 in breast and ovarian tumours. This clearly indicates that driver, trigger or passenger mutations only exert an effect in certain tissues.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk discusses tissue- and cell-type specificity of genetic alterations in cancer. Specific examples cited include APC mutations in colorectal cancer [S1], CDH1 (E-cadherin) in gastric carcinoma [S1], VHL in renal carcinoma [S1|S5], and BCR/ABL translocation in leukaemia/leucocytes [S1|S5]. The authors propose that higher incidence of somatic mutations in certain cell types may stem from cell-specific chromosomal disposition during interphase [S3] and epigenetic imprinting that modulates carcinogen access to DNA [S4]. Germline mutations such as BRCA1/2 and VHL (Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome), among ~30 others, are organism-wide yet predominantly tumourigenic in specific tissues (breast/ovary for BRCA1/2) [S6]. The conclusion is that driver, trigger, or passenger mutations exert oncogenic effects only in specific tissues [S7].

findings.claim: Clear-cell sarcoma -> characteristic chromosomal translocations identified
findings.verbatim_support: The specific morphological patterns observed in human tumours have helped to identify distinct genetic changes: for example, characteristic chromosomal translocations have been identified in desmoplastic round-cell tumours, clear-cell sarcoma, synovial sarcoma and rhabdoid tumours. -42 Moreover, a simple haematoxylin and eosin stain can indicate the presence of a number of hereditary tumours with specific genetic alterations, such as medullary thyroid carcinoma, multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN), the cribriformmorular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma, familial adenomatous polyposis, medullary breast carcinoma, familial breast cancer associated with specific BRCA1 mutations, renal carcinoma, associated with SDHB mutations which shows flocculent cytoplasmic vacuoles, hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer syndrome, and sebaceous lesions associated with Muir -Torre syndrome in colon cancer. Thus, hereditary cancer predisposition syndromes can be identified by immunohistochemistry, which has emerged as a cost-effective strategy (see Table 1).

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk discusses the diagnostic utility of morphological patterns and ancillary techniques in identifying hereditary tumour syndromes and their underlying genetic alterations. Characteristic chromosomal translocations have been identified in desmoplastic round-cell tumours, clear-cell sarcoma, synovial sarcoma, and rhabdoid tumours [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27822]. A simple H&E stain can reveal the presence of numerous hereditary tumours with specific genetic alterations, including medullary thyroid carcinoma, MEN, cribriform-morular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma, familial adenomatous polyposis, medullary breast carcinoma, familial breast cancer with BRCA1 mutations, SDHB mutation-associated renal carcinoma (which shows characteristic flocculent cytoplasmic vacuoles), hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer syndrome, and sebaceous lesions associated with Muir-Torre syndrome in colon cancer [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27822]. Additionally, immunohistochemistry has emerged as a cost-effective strategy for identifying hereditary cancer predisposition syndromes [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27822].

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk addresses intratumour heterogeneity across tumour types. Heterogeneity at the morphological, molecular, and proteomic levels is a near-universal feature of tumours [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27827]. In melanoma specifically, BRAF mutation heterogeneity is observed in more than 10% of cases, meaning the mutation status (wild-type vs mutant) can differ depending on which zone of the tumour is biopsied — an observation with direct clinical implications [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27827]. This principle of intratumoural molecular heterogeneity extends to other clinically relevant biomarkers, including EGFR mutations in NSCLC and ALK rearrangements [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27827].

findings.claim: Field cancerisation may display premalignant histological changes such as dysplasia; many genetic alterations occur without cytological changes
findings.verbatim_support: Molecular and preneoplastic changes in the context of the adjacent tissue: field cancerisation may display premalignant histological changes such as dysplasia; furthermore, many genetic alterations occur without cytological changes. These environmental changes can affect tumour progression by exerting evolutionary pressure on tumour cells and ultimately determining which mutations are selected. Examples of preneoplastic histological lesions include dysplasia (cytological atypia, large hyperchromatic nuclei or nucleoli) and in-situ carcinomas (with no basement membrane invasion), which are observed in most carcinomas. It is noteworthy that some early neoplastic lesions such as colon adenomas and skin naevi are polyclonal. Progression to cancer probably involves the accumulation of multiple field cancerisation driver mutations among synergistically acting groups of mutations. In this regard, molecular studies of peritumour areas in normal ducts of the breast or prostate may show a high number of genetic alterations and driver mutations. The clinical meaning of these molecular changes remains unknown, and further large studies are needed to establish their correlation with tumour relapse. Nonetheless, two important conclusions can be drawn: (i) the study of non-tumour tissue can be relevant in predicting prognosis and risk of second or multiple neoplasia and (ii) we must be very cautious making a diagnosis of malignancy based only on molecular data, as not all mutations in, for example, driver genes, are directly linked to cancer development.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk addresses field cancerisation and preneoplastic changes in the context of tumour-adjacent tissue [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Field cancerisation may exhibit premalignant histological changes such as dysplasia, while many genetic alterations arise without any cytological changes. Environmental shifts in the tumour microenvironment exert evolutionary pressure that shapes mutation selection and tumour progression [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Preneoplastic lesions include dysplasia (characterised by cytological atypia, large hyperchromatic nuclei, or nucleoli) and in-situ carcinomas (lacking basement membrane invasion), both observed across most carcinoma types [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Notably, some early neoplastic lesions — including colon adenomas and skin naevi — are polyclonal [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Cancer progression likely requires accumulation of multiple synergistic driver mutations [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Molecular studies of peritumour normal ducts in breast and prostate tissue can reveal a high burden of genetic alterations and driver mutations [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828], though the clinical significance of these changes with respect to tumour relapse remains undefined [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Two practical conclusions are drawn: (i) analysis of non-tumour tissue may help predict prognosis and second neoplasia risk; and (ii) not all driver gene mutations are causally linked to cancer, urging caution when diagnosing malignancy on molecular data alone [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828].

S1 establishes that some mixed endometrial carcinomas harbour both endometrioid and serous components at the microscopic level, and that molecular analysis of microdissected tissue demonstrates distinct mutational profiles in each component [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27835]. findings.claim: Biphasic synovial sarcoma, carcinosarcomas, and some mesotheliomas exhibit extreme microscopic diversity as mixed tumours
findings.verbatim_support: In some mixed tumours the microscopic diversity is extreme. This is the case in biphasic synovial sarcoma, carcinosarcomas and some mesotheliomas. In carcinosarcomas (named differently in different organs: metaplastic carcinoma, sarcomatoid carcinoma, carcinosarcoma) the malignant epithelial component gives rise to mesenchymal elements, and may even contain fully developed sarcomatoid features, such as malignant skeletal muscle, cartilage or bone elements. Integration of the molecular features into the appropriate microscopic context is essential to understand these tumours and accurately assess prognosis.

In carcinosarcomas (named differently in different organs: metaplastic carcinoma, sarcomatoid carcinoma, carcinosarcoma) the malignant epithelial component gives rise to mesenchymal elements, and may even contain fully developed sarcomatoid features, such as malignant skeletal muscle, cartilage or bone elements. Integration of the molecular features into the appropriate microscopic context is essential to understand these tumours and accurately assess prognosis.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk describes microscopic and molecular features of mixed tumours with extreme histological diversity. Biphasic synovial sarcoma, carcinosarcomas, and some mesotheliomas are identified as prototypic examples of such extreme diversity [S1–S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27836]. Carcinosarcomas—variously termed metaplastic carcinoma, sarcomatoid carcinoma, or carcinosarcoma depending on organ—are characterised by a malignant epithelial component that gives rise to mesenchymal elements and may exhibit fully developed sarcomatoid features such as malignant skeletal muscle, cartilage, or bone [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27836]. Integration of molecular data into the microscopic context is emphasised as essential for understanding these tumours and accurately assessing prognosis [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27836].

findings.claim: BRAF inhibitors -> effective in melanoma with BRAF mutations
findings.verbatim_support: Currently, precision oncology is based on the existence of alterations in certain specific therapeutic targets regardless of tumour location or type. Tumours with somatic mutations such as BRAF, EGFR or gene rearrangements such as ALK are considered therapeutic options regardless of tumour type or location, and tumours may even be characterised as BRAFomas or ALKomas. However, some clinical data have shown that, while BRAF inhibitors are effective in melanoma, the same inhibitors of the same BRAF mutations in colorectal cancer induce feedback loops in signalling pathways that can have a detrimental effect. Cell signalling pathways are also highly regulated, often dependent on numerous positive and negative feedback loops, which are specific to the cell type and tumour environment. For this reason, BRAF inhibition in colorectal cancer indirectly results in EGFR receptor activation and subsequent PI3K -Akt pathway activation. Similarly, ALK alterations and their inhibitors do not have the same clinical response in lung tumours as in neuroblastomas. Further examples are inhibitors of EGFR, HER2 and HER3, depending on the tumour type and location. In a recent basket clinical trial, not all tumours were affected by the same HER mutations, and response to the HER2 inhibitor (neratinib) varied in different tissues: for example, colorectal or bladder cancer with HER2 mutations did not respond. In summary, specific drug treatment depends on the tissue context.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk discusses tissue-context dependency in precision oncology. BRAF inhibitors are effective in BRAF-mutant melanoma [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837] but induce detrimental feedback loops in colorectal cancer [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837], specifically by indirectly activating EGFR and the downstream PI3K-Akt pathway [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. ALK inhibitors yield different clinical responses in lung tumours compared to neuroblastomas [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. In a basket clinical trial, neratinib (HER2 inhibitor) showed variable responses across tumour types, with colorectal and bladder cancers harbouring HER2 mutations failing to respond [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. The overarching conclusion is that specific drug treatment depends on tissue context [S9|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837].

findings.claim: mRNA-based expression studies have low reproducibility dependent on mRNA stability
findings.verbatim_support: Molecular classification based on mRNA expression profiling of gene groups is a frequent approach to identify and classify molecular subtypes of tumours. One of the major achievements of molecular classification has been the subcategorisation according to prognosis, and it is instrumental for the identification of new genetic alterations. However, mRNA-based expression studies are often limited by a low reproducibility, depending on mRNA stability. Furthermore, single-cell sequencing approaches are not feasible in routine diagnostics. Currently, samples are sequenced as the bulk of tumour cells and therefore do not provide information on ITH. In addition to these technical issues, monitoring gene expression at the mRNA level does not necessarily correlate with the function of a protein within a cell, as many post-transcriptional modifications determine whether or not mRNA finally gives rise to a functional protein. Importantly, however, the different molecular subtypes based on enormous mRNA expression matrices can be validated according to protein or gene expression using just a few in-situ hybridisation or IHC probes in most molecular cancer subtypes (see Table 2).

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk discusses the methodological landscape of mRNA-based molecular classification in oncology. While molecular subtyping based on mRNA expression profiling enables prognostic subcategorisation and identification of new genetic alterations [S1–S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838], it carries several technical limitations: mRNA studies have low reproducibility due to mRNA instability [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838], single-cell sequencing is not feasible in routine diagnostics [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838], and bulk sequencing fails to capture intra-tumour heterogeneity (ITH) [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Furthermore, mRNA expression levels do not necessarily reflect protein function, owing to post-transcriptional modifications [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Despite these limitations, molecular subtypes defined by large mRNA expression matrices can generally be validated using a small number of IHC or in-situ hybridisation probes across most molecular cancer subtypes [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838].

findings.claim: Breast carcinoma -> 6 molecular subtypes by mRNA expression profile: luminal A, luminal B, HER2+, basal-like, claudin-low, normal breast-like
findings.verbatim_support: Breast carcinoma. According to the mRNA expression profile, six molecular subtypes are described: luminal A, luminal B, HER2 +, basal-like, claudin-low and normal breast-like. However, RNA signatures can vary dramatically between patients with the same molecular subtype 69 and, with the exception of the basal subtype, are not highly reproducible for diagnosis on microarray analysis. A high degree of ITH has been described, as assessed by immunohistochemical (IHC) studies, array-CGH studies 71 and massive parallel sequencing technologies. Given these problems in the exact diagnosis of breast cancer subtype by molecular characterisation, IHC-based characterisations are recommended as a diagnostic approach in most of the consensus oncology guidelines. Additional IHC staining helps to distinguish luminal A and B subtypes, such as GATA3 and FOXM. CK5 and EGFR expression define the basal subtype of breast cancer, and CD44 and Snail expression determine the claudin-low subtype. Finally, the normal breast-like subtype is defined by low expression of the above-mentioned markers and expression of factors such as CD36 in a low-grade histological tumour.
findings.outcome_entity: molecular subtypes (luminal A, luminal B, HER2+, basal-like, claudin-low, normal breast-like)

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk reviews the molecular and IHC classification of breast carcinoma. Six molecular subtypes are defined by mRNA expression profiling: luminal A, luminal B, HER2+, basal-like, claudin-low, and normal breast-like [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27839]. RNA signatures show high inter-patient variability and are not reliably reproducible on microarray analysis, except for the basal subtype [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27839]. A high degree of intratumoral heterogeneity (ITH) has been documented via IHC, array-CGH, and massive parallel sequencing [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27839]. Consequently, IHC-based classification is recommended by consensus oncology guidelines [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27839]. Key IHC markers include: GATA3 and FOXM for luminal A/B distinction [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27839]; CK5 and EGFR for the basal subtype; CD44 and Snail for the claudin-low subtype [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27839]; and CD36 (with low expression of the above markers) in the low-grade normal breast-like subtype [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27839].

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk addresses molecular subtyping of colorectal carcinoma (CRC). CRC molecular subtypes are distinguished by genomic, epigenetic, and transcriptomic parameters [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27840]. Four consensus molecular subtypes (CMS1–4) have been operationalized by IHC [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27840] using a four-protein panel — CDX2, FRMD6, HTR2B, and ZEB1 — to classify tumors as CMS4 (mesenchymal), CMS1 (immune), or CMS2/3 (epithelial) [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27840]. CMS4 carries the worst prognosis among these subtypes [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27840]. Across all subtypes, driver and actionable genes including RAS and BRAF must be evaluated per approved protocols [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27840].

findings.claim: Glioblastoma -> 4 molecular subtypes based on gene expression profile: proneural, mesenchymal, mixed, unknown
findings.verbatim_support: Glioblastomas. Four molecular subtypes have been described based on gene expression profile: proneural, mesenchymal, mixed and unknown, and up to six based on methylation arrays, recurrent driver genes and transcriptomics, by the DKFZ (Deutsches Krebsforschungs-zentrum). -89 These molecular subtypes are used currently in clinical oncology guides. In brief, according to the most recent World Health Organisation (WHO) classification, grade IV gliomas are classified as IDH-mutant GB, IDH-wt GB and midline glioma with H3 K27M mutation. In order to discriminate between subtypes the following can be analysed using IHC, fluorescence in-situ hybridisation (FISH) or PCR: IDH1/IDH2, ATRX, TP53, FGFR, NF1, H3.1 and H3.3 mutations, EGFR and PDGFR amplifications, BRAF V600 mutation or translocations and CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletion.

findings.claim: Bladder cancer RNA genome-wide studies characterise two main molecular groups (basal and luminal subtypes) with prognostic and predictive impact
findings.verbatim_support: Urothelial bladder carcinoma. Different molecular classifications are currently being explored. One of them, based on RNA genomewide studies, has characterised two main molecular groups of bladder cancer with prognostic and predictive impact. Group 1 basal subtype includes a subgroup of claudin-low and is characterised by expression of the basal cytokeratins CK5, CK14 and CD44. Group 2 luminal subtype has mutations of the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene and urothelial differentiation markers such as CK20, GATA3 and uroplakins. The luminal subtype has a more favourable prognosis than the basal subtype. Recently, a prospective multicentre validation study with a 12-gene signature progression score in nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer was demonstrated to have independent prognostic power beyond clinical and histopathological risk factors, and could help in stratifying patients to optimise treatment and followup. Other molecular alterations have also been described, such as FGFR3 mutations in 80%, PI3KCA mutations in approximately 20% and mutations in the core promoter region of the human telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) gene in up to 85% of bladder tumours. Interestingly, FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations have been demonstrated as biomarkers on liquid biopsy for disease surveillance for bladder cancer. Different cell cycle genes may be altered in invasive urothelial carcinoma, mainly tumour suppressor genes, including TP53, p16 and Rb. Finally, combinations of TP53, p21, p27 and pRb proved to be more precise in classifying bladder cancer patients into risk groups.
findings.outcome_entity: two main molecular groups (basal and luminal subtypes)

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk covers the molecular classification of urothelial bladder carcinoma (PMC6851567). RNA genome-wide studies define two main molecular subtypes with prognostic and predictive relevance [S3]. The **basal subtype (Group 1)** includes a claudin-low subgroup and is characterised by expression of CK5, CK14, and CD44 [S4]. The **luminal subtype (Group 2)** harbours FGFR3 mutations and expresses urothelial differentiation markers CK20, GATA3, and uroplakins [S5]. Crucially, the luminal subtype carries a more favourable prognosis compared to the basal subtype [S6]. A prospective multicentre validation study showed that a 12-gene signature progression score in non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer has independent prognostic power beyond clinical and histopathological risk factors [S7]. Key molecular alterations include FGFR3 mutations (~80%), PIK3CA mutations (~20%), and TERT core promoter mutations (up to 85%) across bladder tumours [S8]; FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations have additionally been validated as liquid biopsy biomarkers for disease surveillance [S9]. In invasive urothelial carcinoma, cell cycle tumour suppressor genes—TP53, p16, and Rb—are frequently altered [S10].

findings.claim: mRNA expression profiles and protein expression levels show discordance due to RNA stability and sampling area variation
findings.verbatim_support: Molecular tumour subtypes based on mRNA expression profiles often show discordance with protein expression levels, depending on the RNA stability and the area sampled. It is well known that RNA studies are problematic regarding reproducibility, and that protein expression shows the real functional status of the targets. A classic example is breast cancer, in which mRNA profiles can define at least six different molecular categories. While this can be used as a general classification scheme, only IHC or FISH analysis of proteins in tumour cells within the individual subgroup can provide the exact diagnosis to guide treatment and prognosis. Some reports 67 describe discord, when comparing mRNA and protein expression levels, of up to 50% of cases in HER2 status, and in more than 15% of cases when distinguishing between luminal A and luminal B.

findings.claim: IHC is currently the most robust readout for intratumour heterogeneity (ITH) assessment
findings.verbatim_support: Currently, the most robust readout for ITH assessment comes from IHC. A classic example is ITH of oestrogen receptors, which may be positive in just 1% of cells; in fact, this ITH has been reported to be associated with long-term risk of fatal breast cancer. Other examples are the heterogeneous expression of cyclin D1 in mantle cell lymphomas, which otherwise carry a homogeneous CCND1 -IGH translocation 107 and the subtype of HER2 + breast or gastric tumours that can range from 10% to 100% positive cells.

findings.claim: Tumour protein expression depends on local microenvironmental factors (hypoxia, nutrient starvation, oxidative stress) independently of cellular genetic background
findings.verbatim_support: Within an entire tumour, protein expression often depends on local factors such as hypoxia, nutrient starvation or oxidative stress, independently of the cell's genetic background. These environmental cues can alter entire signalling pathways downstream of well-established oncogenic alterations. Many tumours may have activating mutations in the most upstream elements of certain signalling cascades, such as RAS, EGFR and HER2, but phosphorylation of downstream factors such as MAP-kinases or mTOR may be inhibited by environmental factors; 110 therefore, even if specific driver genetic alterations are inhibited, no effect will be observed in cells in which these signalling pathways are inhibited by such factors.

Protein expression within a tumour is shaped by local conditions such as hypoxia, nutrient starvation, and oxidative stress, independent of genetic background [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27850]. findings.claim: Primary tumours -> heterogeneous epithelial cell content; form ecosystem with stromal cells, endothelial cells, leucocytes, lymphocytes, histiocytes, and secreted factors
findings.verbatim_support: Primary tumours have heterogeneous epithelial cell content, and form an ecosystem with the environmental cells, including stromal cells, endothelial cells, leucocytes, lymphocytes, histiocytes and their secreted factors. In a pathological context, we can quantify and evaluate the expression of the immune checkpoints programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) and programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) in epithelial and inflammatory parts of the tumour and use this information for clinical correlation studies. Similar to cell signalling pathways, key components of immune checkpoints, such as PD-L1, can also have heterogeneous expression throughout the tumour. The PDL1 protein is expressed in a wide range of cell types, including lymphocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells, and is stimulated by variable and complex mechanisms. In contrast to other immune checkpoint components, PD-L1 is rarely expressed in normal tissue but is induced in tumour-associated tissue, is a tumour biomarker and is also an attractive drug target. As many current treatment schemes are based on immunotherapy, pathological assessment should include immune checkpoint proteins. Furthermore, the heterogeneous and dynamic expression of factors such as PD-L1 in basal conditions and in response to different treatments presents a challenge to predicting which patients will respond to antiPDL1 therapies. The assessment of CD4 +, CD8 + cells, and tumour mutational burden (TMB) can also be helpful in clinical decision-making. TMB has recently been proposed as a new biomarker to quantify the potential tumoral neoantigenicity, with the aim of predicting patients who will benefit from immunocheckpoint inhibitors. Nevertheless, different technologies and different thresholds have been proposed to define high versus low TMB in different tissue samples. -117
findings.outcome_entity: heterogeneous epithelial cell content / tumour microenvironment ecosystem

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk from PMC6851567 (HIS-75-4) provides a conceptual overview of immune checkpoint biology and its pathological assessment. Primary tumours exhibit heterogeneous epithelial cell content and form a complex ecosystem with stromal, endothelial, immune, and secreted-factor components [S1]. PD-L1 and PD-1 can be quantified in both epithelial and inflammatory tumour compartments for clinical correlation [S2]. PD-L1 expression is itself heterogeneous throughout the tumour [S3], is broadly expressed in lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells via complex stimulatory mechanisms [S4], and — in contrast to other checkpoint components — is rarely expressed in normal tissue but is induced in tumour-associated tissue, qualifying it as both a biomarker and drug target [S5]. Given widespread immunotherapy adoption, pathological assessment should incorporate immune checkpoint proteins [S6]. The dynamic and heterogeneous nature of PD-L1 expression, both at baseline and in response to treatment, complicates response prediction for anti-PD-L1 therapies [S7]. CD4+/CD8+ assessment and tumour mutational burden (TMB) also contribute to clinical decision-making [S8]; TMB is specifically proposed as a neoantigenicity biomarker for predicting benefit from immune checkpoint inhibitors [S9], though high/low TMB thresholds remain inconsistent across technologies and tissue types [S10].

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk establishes general principles of histological classification and grading in oncology. Histological subtype determination is prognostically critical: in lung carcinoma, prognosis and treatment differ substantially between small-cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and large-cell carcinoma [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27856]; similarly, ovarian carcinoma survival varies widely across high-/low-grade serous, endometrioid, clear-cell, and mucinous adenocarcinoma subtypes [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27856]. Tumour grading into high- and low-grade categories is determined by cell differentiation, cellular atypia, and proliferation [S3–S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27856]. Ki-67 serves as a proliferation index to quantify replicative cells within tumours [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27856] and is detectable irrespective of the underlying genetic alterations driving proliferation [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27856]. These classical morphological grading criteria have been validated by RNA and molecular data [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27856].

findings.verbatim_support: As described above, cellular stress can alter gene expression in tumour cells at several levels modifying biochemical signalling pathways and feedback loops, and protein expression can be heterogenous. Cellular stress can alter gene expression and signalling pathways within tumour cells, leading to heterogeneous protein expression [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27857]. findings.claim: Multiple oncogenic events converge on cellular networks containing clinically targetable hubs (e.g., eIF4F complex)
findings.verbatim_support: Systems biology encompasses tools that hold great promise for deciphering the vulnerabilities of the tumour ecosystem as a whole. Studies are based on the premise that multiple oncogenic events converge on a number of cellular networks that may contain essential or synthetically lethal clinically targetable hubs or factors, such as the eIF4F complex. Nonetheless, many contemporary systems biology approaches do not consider intratumour heterogeneity. This is relevant because key functional nodes within the metabolic, signal transduction and gene expression networks responsible for supporting the tumour phenotype are critically dependent on the heterogeneity of the tumour. These data can also help to classify tumours according to histopathological, biochemical and genomic features and thus help to tailor the diagnosis and clinical management to a patient's biological tumour profile. Accordingly, multidimensional molecular and gene expression data, which are associated with the response to antitumour treatments and clinical progress, are thought to facilitate the selection of patients who are more likely to respond to targeted or 'precise' therapies. -131 The availability of systemwide data in a variety of cancers is facilitating the development of approaches that go beyond the classic, reductionist paradigms that associate single genes with cellular phenotypes and functions. Systems biology approaches consider the interplay between multiple molecular factors that underpin phenotype development. Accordingly, rather than a genetic disease, cancer is now perceived as a disease of 'networks', and to fully grasp the complexity of the tumour ecosystem the networks driving cancer need to be mapped and their dynamics and evolution over time deciphered. map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk (PMC6851567, C1) presents a conceptual framework for systems biology in oncology. Multiple oncogenic events converge on targetable cellular network hubs such as the eIF4F complex [S2]. A key limitation of current systems biology approaches is their failure to incorporate intratumour heterogeneity [S3], which is critical because tumour phenotype-supporting network nodes depend on this heterogeneity [S4]. Cancer is reframed as a disease of 'networks' rather than a purely genetic disease [S9], and these networks are continuously rewired by clonal interactions, microenvironmental changes, and treatment-induced molecular alterations [S10]. Multidimensional molecular and gene expression data are thought to predict response to targeted therapies [S6], and histopathological, biochemical, and genomic tumour classification can enable personalised clinical management [S5].

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk addresses two interrelated concepts in cancer biology and treatment. First [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27862], minor tumour subpopulations — undetectable in bulk tumour analysis but capable of environmental adaptation — may selectively emerge after therapies that target cancer-driving mutations in dominant subpopulations, illustrating a mechanism of acquired treatment resistance driven by intratumoural heterogeneity (ITH). Second [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27862], systems biology is proposed as a critical future tool for: (i) clinically oriented cancer subclassification, (ii) mapping oncogenic networks and pinpointing key nodes to overcome ITH, and (iii) anticipating therapy response in silico to guide preclinical research, Phase I trial design, and personalised/precision medicine target selection.

findings.claim: Liquid biopsy analytes include circulating tumour cells (CTCs), plasma-derived cell-free tumour DNA (cfDNA), RNA, and DNA from circulating tumour exosomes in blood
findings.verbatim_support: As biopsies are associated with a degree of invasiveness and cannot always be repeated, new approaches have been proposed, such as the analysis of circulating tumour cells (CTCs), plasma-derived cell-free tumour DNA (cfDNA) or RNA and, more recently, DNA from circulating tumour exosomes in blood. -135 This strategy enables a global assessment of the constellation of somatic genetic alterations in a tumour irrespective of its anatomical location, and is becoming a good alternative for the study of a tumour mutational landscape in situations where biopsies or surgical samples are difficult to obtain. Hence, liquid biopsy appears to be a very relevant tool for the identification of potential actionable genomic alterations and therapeutic targets, monitoring treatment response, predicting disease progression before clinical and radiological confirmation and identifying mechanisms of resistance in the particular context of patients with early-stage and metastatic disease. Furthermore, liquid biopsy provides additional cues on ITH, as reported in a recent pilot study in patients with early-stage NSCLC.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk describes the utility of liquid biopsy in oncology. Liquid biopsy analytes — including CTCs, cfDNA, RNA, and circulating tumour exosome DNA — enable global, location-independent assessment of the tumour mutational landscape and are emerging as an alternative to tissue biopsies when these are difficult to obtain [S1–S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27863]. Key clinical applications include identification of actionable genomic alterations and therapeutic targets, monitoring treatment response, predicting disease progression ahead of clinical/radiological confirmation, and characterising resistance mechanisms, particularly in early-stage and metastatic disease [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27863].
